title: Two are better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)
hook: if one falls, the other lifts; a threefold cord is not quickly broken

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's list of seasons, and your line was a time to speak. What time is it for you this week? Day four hundred fifty-six.

Right before today's passage, the Preacher describes a man who has no one. No child, no brother. And there's no end to his work, the text says, and his eyes are never satisfied with his money. He never stops to ask who all this is for. It's a sharp little portrait, and it could be someone you know: the one who answers emails at midnight, eats at the desk, and hasn't called a friend in a year. The Preacher has been looking hard at everything under the sun and finding most of it breath. But then, in the middle of all that hevel, he finds something that holds. Today, the thing that holds.
screen: `A MAN WITH NO ONE.` → `NO END TO HIS WORK.` → `WHO IS THIS FOR?` → `SOMETHING THAT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Then the Preacher gives three pictures, all very physical. First, the fall: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." A road at night, a ditch, a twisted ankle. Second, the cold: two people lying together keep each other warm, but how can one be warm alone? Third, the attack: someone might overpower a person alone, but two can stand against him. Fall, cold, danger. In each one, a second person is the difference. Then, almost as a proverb tacked on the end, the line your carry comes from: "and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Twist two strands together and they're stronger. Twist in a third and the rope holds far more. Notice the Preacher counted two, and then the proverb says three. Readers have wondered about that. At Christian weddings, the third strand is often heard as God, woven in with the couple. Others hear it simply as a proverb about community: two is good, more is better. The text itself doesn't say who the third strand is. But it's a striking moment. The Preacher who called everything breath doesn't call friendship breath. In a book that doubts almost everything, he's sure of this.
screen: `A MAN ALONE, WORKING FOR NO ONE.` · `IF ONE FALLS, THE OTHER LIFTS.` · `TWO KEEP WARM; TWO STAND FIRM.` · `A THREEFOLD CORD.` · then, large: `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a friend, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who once lifted you when you fell: a hard week, a bad diagnosis, a breakup, a day you couldn't get off the couch. See their face. Remember one specific thing they did, the call, the meal, the ride, the hour they just sat there. Notice how that time might have gone alone. Then think of the words you'd use to thank them, simple and plain. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Two are better than one. The Preacher's three pictures: one to lift, one to warm, one to stand beside you, and a cord of three strands that does not quickly break.
screen: `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a threefold cord. Today, look for one person carrying something alone, and be the second strand: one call, one ride, one hour of company. Day four hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 is a common reading at Christian weddings, where the threefold cord is often explained as husband, wife and God; some couples braid three cords during the ceremony.

fork.setup: you're traveling alone at night and fall into a ditch. what does the Preacher say about this moment?
options: climb out yourself: that's what strength is.
woe to the one who is alone, with no one to help him up.

fork.reveal: "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." the Preacher's answer to a fall is a friend.

original.note: Hebrew: the threefold cord, a thread twisted from three strands.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wedding saying about God and a couple.
what it means: companionship holds you up in a fall, keeps you warm, and stands with you in danger.
what a scholar hears: the count moves from two to three, a pattern used in Hebrew sayings to build to a climax. the text never names the third strand.

notes: Editor pass (y2 review): 'no son' corrected to the KJV 'neither child nor brother' (4:8); cut the unsourced desert-travelers gloss and 'how rope is actually made'; 'many Christians' softened; the practice no longer tells the listener what to feel. The carry changed from 'send the thank-you' to being the second strand for someone, because day 453's carry already had the listener thank someone and day 458 has them tell someone they love them.
Hebrew for 'the threefold cord': הַחוּט הַמְשֻׁלָּשׁ (ha-chut ha-meshullash). Confirm spelling, pointing and transliteration.
'Desert nights get cold, travelers shared blankets': a general cultural gloss on 4:11; confirm or soften.
The trapdoor's 'two-then-three' as a Hebrew climactic pattern (cf. the x / x+1 numerical sayings of Proverbs 30) is an interpretive observation; confirm it is fair to apply here.
Wedding custom of braiding three cords ('cord of three strands' ceremony) is a modern evangelical practice; confirm howItsDone.
